analysis.one_liner: Lets states and cities suing gun makers also recover the federal costs of gun violence.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 1999 with four Democratic senators behind it, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: In the late 1990s, cities and states were suing gun manufacturers to recover the costs of gun violence. This bill would have let those governments add the federal government's costs — taxpayer-funded medical care, disability, law enforcement, and lost wages — to their lawsuits. Two-thirds of any money recovered would stay with the state or city for law enforcement, victim compensation, schools, child care, and children's health care; one-third would go to the federal government for crime prevention and injury research.
analysis.who_benefits: State and local governments bring the suits, so they control the claims, and their communities get the money: a victims' compensation fund, aid for injured officers' families, smaller classes and school repairs, child care, and children's health care. Federal taxpayers also benefit, since the bill's own findings say at least 80 percent of the cost of treating firearm injuries is paid with taxpayer dollars [S3].

how_it_helps.text: In any state or local government lawsuit against a firearm manufacturer over the sale, distribution, use, or misuse of guns, the government could recover 'Federal damages' — the federal government's costs from gun violence, including medical expenses, continuing care, law enforcement costs, and lost wages [S2] [S3].

Of the money recovered, two-thirds stays with the state or local government: one third for law enforcement, families of officers killed or injured by gun violence, and a victims' compensation fund; one third for education (smaller classes, school modernization, after-school and tutoring), child care, or children's health care; one third at the government's discretion. The remaining one-third goes to the federal government for crime prevention, mentoring, and firearm injury research [S3].

The bill is framed as an incentive for governments to bring claims that force the industry to change how it makes and distributes guns, citing the industry's refusal to include safety devices like child safety locks and distribution practices that oversupply legal markets feeding illegal ones [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers — and by extension distributors and retailers — would face new monetary liability whenever a state or city wins or settles a gun-violence lawsuit against them. The bill's own findings tie the claims to industry marketing and distribution practices, so the money would come from the industry's sales of the products involved [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill creates no direct safety rules; it works only through litigation, so recoveries depend on courts agreeing that manufacturers are liable for the misuse of a lawful product — a contested legal theory — and the whole scheme fails if those suits do not succeed [S3].

It applies to lawsuits already pending when the bill passes, as long as the government amends its complaint to add the federal damages claim, which critics would call adding new liability to old cases [S3].

It puts Washington in the middle of local lawsuits: the Attorney General is served notice and can take over the federal portion of any claim, and state and local governments cannot both recover federal damages for the same area — the first to file wins [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design channels real public costs — hospital care, policing, victims' compensation — back onto the industry whose products caused them, and the mandatory spending on victims, schools, and child care is unusually concrete. But it is an indirect tool: nothing changes unless governments sue, courts agree the industry is liable, and money actually comes back. A supporter would admit the recoveries are speculative; the honest case is that it was a low-cost lever to press the industry toward safety features and tighter distribution.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in March 1999, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no vote — before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Frank Lautenberg introduced the Gun Industry Accountability Act on March 8, 1999; Sen. Tom Daschle introduced it on his behalf, joined by Sens. Durbin, Schumer, and Reed [S5] [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
The action history records no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind for the rest of the Congress [S5].

The bill arrived in the middle of a wave of city and state lawsuits against the gun industry; its stated purpose was to give those governments an added incentive by letting them recover the federal government's costs of gun violence [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers and sellers avoided the added liability the bill would have created, while the cities and states suing them got no new tool and taxpayers kept absorbing the costs of gun violence.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers who avoided new liability

for.name: Sen. Frank R. Lautenberg

for.name: Sens. Dick Durbin, Chuck Schumer, and Jack Reed
Sen. Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on Lautenberg's behalf, which flagged it as a leadership priority.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died there.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee consideration of the bill during the 106th Congress.

against.name: Gun manufacturers and the National Rifle Association
against.role: Firearm industry and its lobbying arm
against.what_they_did: Opposed the late-1990s wave of municipal lawsuits against the gun industry that this bill was designed to reinforce, and pushed Congress for protections against such suits.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats, introduced by the Senate's Democratic leader; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee gave it no consideration.

industries.note: The bill would have made them financially responsible, through state and city lawsuits, for the federal costs of gun violence tied to their products — medical care, policing, lost wages. It matters for ordinary people because the bill's findings say taxpayers cover at least 80 percent of the cost of treating firearm injuries, and the prospect of liability was the lever meant to force safety features like child locks and tighter distribution.
